lead: Rolling passes a strip between two rotating rolls set closer than the strip is thick. Friction at the roll surface drags the strip into the gap; the strip leaves thinner and longer. This one idea makes most flat steel: car bodies, food cans, roofing sheet, and railway rails by shape rolling. It is the highest-volume bulk forming process because it is continuous, fast and cheap per tonne. The same mechanics explain why a heavy pass may refuse to enter the rolls, and why rolled sheet can have wavy edges or a buckled centre.
prereq: You need: 2.1 for flow stress and the hot–cold split.

sections.h3: The roll bite and the friction condition

blocks.text: Two rolls of radius R (mm) turn toward each other. The gap is set to the exit thickness h₁ (mm); the entry strip is h₀ (mm). The draft is Δh = h₀ − h₁, in mm. The strip touches each roll along an arc of horizontal length L (mm). For shallow bites, L ≈ √(RΔh). The bite angle α is the angle between the entry point and the roll centre line.

Friction pulls the strip in; the roll also pushes it back. The strip enters only if μ ≥ tan α, where μ is the coefficient of friction (no unit). For small α, tan α ≈ √(Δh/R). Squaring gives Δh ≤ μ²R. So Δh<sub>max</sub> = μ²R. Use the radius R, never the diameter.

blocks.where: Δh<sub>max</sub> is the largest thickness reduction in one pass (mm); μ is the coefficient of friction (no unit); R is the roll radius (mm).
L is the contact length along the arc (mm); R is the roll radius (mm); Δh = h₀ − h₁ is the draft (mm).

blocks.text: Near entry the strip is slower than the roll surface: backward slip. At the neutral point strip speed equals roll surface speed. After it the strip is faster: forward slip. Forward slip = (v<sub>exit</sub> − v<sub>roll</sub>)/v<sub>roll</sub>, where v<sub>exit</sub> is exit strip speed and v<sub>roll</sub> is roll surface speed.

A two-high mill has two rolls. A reversing two-high mill runs the strip back and forth. A three-high mill passes the strip between top and middle rolls one way, then middle and bottom rolls the other way. A four-high mill uses two small work rolls backed by two large rolls that stop bending. A cluster mill, such as a Sendzimir mill, supports small work rolls with many backup rolls for very thin hard strip. A tandem mill has several stands in line, one pass each.

Hot rolling starts with a reheated slab. A reversing roughing mill breaks it down; a finishing train of four-high stands rolls it to coil thickness; a run-out table sprays water; a down coiler winds the strip. Hot rolling is above the recrystallisation temperature, so the metal is soft and the surface carries oxide scale. Cold rolling is at room temperature. It gives better finish and tolerance, but work-hardens the metal, so annealing is needed between passes. Roll camber and roll bending control crown, the small centre-to-edge thickness difference.
Flat rolling makes plate, sheet and strip. Shape rolling makes rails and sections; some syllabi use these two names. Roll pass design for sections is left to a dedicated course.

Rolled strip has named defects. Wavy edges: edges elongate more than the centre, so the extra length buckles into waves. Centre buckle: the centre elongates more, so the middle lifts. Edge cracking: edges are held back and tear. Alligatoring: a horizontal split at a slab end because surface and centre deform differently. Laps and seams: folded metal or cracks along the strip. Scale: oxide pressed into a hot-rolled surface. Roll marks: repeating marks from a damaged roll.

Rolled products: a bloom, a large square section; a billet, a smaller square section; a slab, a wide rectangle for flat products; plate, thick flat product; sheet, thin flat product; strip, sheet in coil form; rail, a shaped product. Bloom, billet and slab are intermediate shapes. Loads are estimated in 2.6; forging and extrusion are in 2.3 and 2.4.

spec.aria: A vertical flow chart of one rolling pass: entry strip 20 mm, roll bite with radius 300 mm and friction 0.10, neutral point, exit strip 15 mm, and result draft 5 mm with contact length 38.7 mm.

examples.question: A 250 mm wide strip is rolled from 20 mm to 15 mm in one pass on rolls of radius 300 mm. The coefficient of friction is 0.10. (a) Is the pass possible? (b) What minimum μ would make it possible? (c) Find the contact length.
steps: Data: h₀ = 20 mm, h₁ = 15 mm, R = 300 mm, μ = 0.10, width b = 250 mm. Width does not enter the bite condition.
Compare: 5 mm > 3 mm, so friction cannot pull the strip in. The pass fails.
examples.answer: The pass is not possible at μ = 0.10; it needs μ ≈ 0.13 or two passes, and L ≈ 38.7 mm.
examples.check:
mu = 0.10
R = 300.0
h0 = 20.0
h1 = 15.0
draft = h0 - h1
dh_max = mu * mu * R
mu_req = (draft / R) ** 0.5
L = (R * draft) ** 0.5
print(int(draft))
print(dh_max)
print(round(mu_req, 2))
print(round(L, 1))

traps: Using the roll diameter in Δh<sub>max</sub> = μ²R. R is the radius; a diameter value doubles the wrong quantity.
Draft is Δh in mm. Reduction ratio is r = Δh/h₀, no unit. A 5 mm draft on a 20 mm strip is r = 0.25, not 5.
A pass with Δh > μ²R cannot be forced by more roll force alone. The strip slips or buckles; change μ, use a smaller draft, or use larger R.
Wavy edges and centre buckle look similar but have opposite causes. Wavy edges: edges longer. Centre buckle: centre longer.
The neutral point is not the middle of the contact arc. It is where strip speed equals roll surface speed; its position moves with friction and tension.

quiz.q: Define draft in rolling and give its formula in terms of entry and exit thickness.
quiz.a: Draft Δh = h₀ − h₁, where h₀ is entry thickness and h₁ is exit thickness, both in mm.
The point on the contact arc where strip speed equals roll surface speed; before it there is backward slip, after it forward slip.

quiz.q: Why is friction necessary in rolling but also a problem?
quiz.a: Friction pulls the strip into the gap; without μ ≥ tan α the pass fails. Too much friction raises roll force, power and surface wear, and can cause defects.

quiz.q: A 10 mm strip is rolled to 7 mm on rolls of radius 250 mm. Find the minimum coefficient of friction and the contact length.
Rolls of radius 200 mm have μ = 0.12. Find the maximum draft in one pass.
A mill has enough force to reduce a strip by 8 mm, but μ²R is only 5 mm. Explain what happens and give two remedies.
quiz.a: The bite condition fails: friction cannot pull the strip through an 8 mm draft. The strip slips or buckles at entry. Remedies: reduce draft to ≤5 mm (more passes), increase μ, or increase R.

quiz.q: Explain why wavy edges and centre buckle occur in rolled sheet, using the idea of uneven elongation.
quiz.a: If edges elongate more than the centre, extra edge length buckles as wavy edges. If the centre elongates more, the centre buckles. Uneven elongation comes from roll bending, camber, or uneven reduction across width.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern hot strip mills use hydraulic gap control and roll bending to hold crown within a few micrometres over a kilometre of strip. Endless rolling and thin-slab casting remove the reheating furnace for some steel grades. Researchers model the roll bite with friction laws that depend on speed and lubricant. Search for roll bite condition, neutral point rolling, crown control, Sendzimir mill, and alligatoring.
